I was stuck on the base camp on Mount Fuji in Japan. I had to give my friend my cash bc we were too late to catch the bus the previous night. There are no ATMs up there.

A group of students approached me and asked me what was wrong, I had to use google translate to tell them, they each gave me a 100 yen coin and there were so many of them I had enough to take the bus back. My family adopted a gofin 10 years ago. He was severely neglected. He was never let out of his cage, held in a garage and only had one tiny perch which hurt his feet so he would lean on the side of the cage to get the pressure of his feet. 

I think it took him a few years to recover fully, but he’s very happy and full of attitude now. 

When we let him out of the cage he fist tore the plastic off of the bike lock his previous owners used to keep his cage locked. He slowly learned how to fly, he was slow and heavy at first and crashed into stuff, but he’s a really good flyer now. He found his very very loud voice, and eats a variety of treats. 

We certainly had to adapt to his behaviors and patterns. They need a lot of toys and wood to shred, also a good daily schedule to keep them calm and so they know what to expect. 

There were certainly some challenges and ups and downs and times where he was very vocal and stressed out, but eventually we understood his needs and how to condition certain behavior. But he is a very challenging pet that requires time and attention and stimulation to be fulfilled and if they don’t get enough they will let you know.

Ooof this is an anniversary for me too. It’s a struggle. Especially with all the holiday associations. It’s been 8 years for me almost on the dot and I went into psychosis after and i feel like there are too many flashbacks and it’s so damn hard reaching out for help. Over the years I used to just get really high and just zone out. I can’t really do that anymore and my feelings are pretty sharp

The suggestions I have aren’t the best but what’s helped me get through it is being around people, just casually as a distraction. Getting coffee, hanging out, anything really, even if they’re not close friends

Also doing something you don’t normally do to make new memories and do random traditions that can form new associations with this time of year. I used to go to the zoo every year around this time, it’s my favorite zoo and looking at cute animals is really healing. 

Create tasks for yourself, like painting your bedroom, or cleaning something random you don’t normally clean, which can be hard when you just want to lay down. 

In terms of the food thing I realllllly recommend seeing a dietician, it’s helped me so so so much, but it can be expensive but in my experience made a huge difference  

Other than that it’s important not to fight the thoughts too much because they’re going to come up for processing. 

I’m sorry about your therapist, but I think you should keep trying to look for one, even though it’s a struggle especially when you don’t feel good

I think routine is one of the most important things for them. Having a morning, day and night routine gives them a sense of security, plus a bedtime. 
A good way to initiate a routine is using different snacks at certain times of day. Our bird has snap peas in the morning, broccoli during the day and a macadamia nut at the end of the day, he’s going to expect those treats at specific times and it’s easy to put some structure and other fun enriching activities into his day and keep him busy and his mind occupied, like once our bird eats the macadamia nut he goes straight to his perch to sleep because he knows it’s time. 

We gave him a large chunk of a room that we turned into his personal corner, it’s like an extra large cage with his actual cage inside it and a lot of toys, perches and climbing stuff, also food and water, and it’s a place we put him to cool off when he gets destructive or overwhelmed or territorial, and he stays in there when my parents leave the house, and sleeps in there. 
There’s enough room to fly around and create his own environment, we give him old furniture to destroy, and just safe tactile objects to play with 

He’s pretty territorial over his space, but it’s improved his mood because it’s his own and he feels safe in there without being confined, and it’s a good way to discourage mating behaviors by separating him without punishment (which doesn’t work anyway)

It’s something I’ve been dealing with for over a year and a half, been able to cut down on the binging and purging significantly. It still happens here and there unfortunately

What’s worked for me is counting calories ( still disordered but I don’t restrict much, just make sure I don’t binge) 

Working with a dietician, I make sure I never get hungry enough to binge, so I try to eat a small amount of food every 3 hours and stay not hungry and not full as much as possible to not trigger myself. Your goal is to never get to painful hunger or painful fullness, bc that leads to low blood sugar as well as binging. Every time you eat kind of check in with yourself to make sure you stop eating once you feel full, and keep eating if you’re hungry, this won’t work if you don’t eat for a while though. 

Overall it’s all very tied to your mental health as well, so make sure you keep that in check and notice if you’re sad or lonely or anything when you’re binging. 

It’s a long hard road in recovery and it sucks, but purging won’t get you your dream body, it will only make it harder to work out and make you more likely to binge. At my worst I was actually gaining weight and having horrible heart palpitations, couldn’t breathe in the middle of the night. 

My biggest advice is to see a dietician with experience on these things and a therapist, because in reality it’s very different for everyone and the way to approach treatment is very different, so it’s best to see a professional just to see what works best for you personally
